Rex had demanded the room be purged of any distractions.
The quiet, methodical preparations had been unnerving; she watched from her perch as he moved with a predator’s economy of motion.
He shoved the small table toward the window with a deliberate scrape that set her teeth on edge, drew the heavy curtains to choke out the afternoon sunlight, and finally knelt on the floor.
He placed a single candle at the room’s center, its flame casting dancing, skeletal shadows across the walls.
According to the archive documentation Elaris had unearthed, soul manipulation required this specific low-light environment to prevent ambient energy from contaminating the spiritual tether.
Rex moved with a calm, unhurried competence that made Iris feel like prey being prepared for ritual slaughter.
She watched him, her chest tight with an emotion that fluctuated violently between a desperate gratitude for his willingness to help and a primal, bone-deep nervousness she hadn’t anticipated.
"You do not have to do this today," Rex said.
His voice was low, carrying that same unshakable authority that always seemed to command her surrender.
He didn’t even look up from where he was kneeling beside the candle, adjusting its position by a fraction of an inch with terrifying precision.
"If you need more time to gather your courage."
"I do not need more time," Iris snapped.
The sharpness of her own voice surprised her, cutting through the heavy silence like a blade.
"I have had twenty-six days of time, Rex..."
"Thirty-two days of waking up with this hollow ache in my chest, wondering if I’ll ever feel whole again."
She took a shuddering breath, her gaze fixed on the flickering candle flame.
"If I wait any longer, I am going to talk myself out of it entirely..."
"I’ll find excuses.
I’ll convince myself that the pain is manageable, that the emptiness is just part of living."
"And I cannot.
I will not lose this chance simply because I let myself get too comfortable with the idea of losing it."
Rex turned his head toward her then, his dark eyes catching the amber glow of the solitary candle.
Something shifted in his expression; the predatory edge softened into something far more dangerous: a quiet, genuine respect.

It was the kind of respect he reserved only for those who possessed the rare fortitude to be brutally honest about their own vulnerabilities, rather than those who donned a mask of false courage to impress him.
A slow, devilish smirk began to tug at the corner of his mouth, breaking the solemnity of the moment.
His gaze raked over her flushed face, lingering on the way her pulse fluttered visibly at the base of her throat.
"Well," he purred, his voice dropping to a husky, teasing register that made her skin prickle.
"I have to hand it to you, Iris."
"After yesterday... after everything we did...
I honestly didn’t think you’d be this eager to get back to work."
"I half expected you to be unable to walk straight today, let alone crave another session with me." He let out a low, amused chuckle, leaning in slightly.
"Most women would need at least twenty-four hours to recover from how hard I fucked you last night.
"But here you are, rushing straight into the fire."
Iris felt the heat explode across her cheeks.
A furious, involuntary blush flooded her entire face, spreading down to her collarbones.
The memory of his relentless thrusts and the way she had begged for more flashed through her mind like a lightning strike, making her stomach flip with shame and arousal all at once.
"Shut up!" she hissed, though the effect was ruined by the breathless tremor in her voice.
"Just shut up, Rex!
This is serious!"
Rex laughed again, a rich, warm sound that filled the cramped, shadowy space, before he composed himself.
The playfulness vanished as quickly as it had appeared, replaced by the focused intensity of a craftsman preparing for a delicate operation.
"Then we begin," he said, his tone turning steel hard.
He moved with fluid grace, crossing the small distance to sit directly across from her on the floor.
He positioned himself so close that his knees nearly brushed the edge of the mattress where she sat.
The proximity was overwhelming; she could feel the heat radiating from his massive frame, the faint scent of musk and sweat still clinging to him.
He reached out, extending both hands toward her, palms upturned.
It was an invitation but also a ritual, the specific, sacred requirement of a soul manipulation working that demanded physical contact to act as a conduit, an anchor between two spirits.
"Give me your hands," he commanded softly.
His eyes locked onto hers, demanding she meet his gaze without flinching.
"And listen to me carefully, Iris."
"Remember what I told you back in the archery yard when your hands were shaking on the bowstring... which is stillness."
"I am not talking about the absence of feeling that is impossible, but it’s more like I am talking about the absence of fighting what you feel."
His fingers twitched slightly in anticipation.
"When this starts, your soul is going to react..."
"It might burn, it might feel like it’s being torn apart, or it might feel like you’re drowning in ice," Rex grinned.
"Do not recoil and do not try to suppress the pain or control the shape of the sensation."
"If you fight it, you will break yourself."
"Let whatever happens... happen.
Let it flow through you without resistance."
Iris tentatively placed her hands in his.
Her palms were ice-cold, not from the draft in the room but from the paralyzing chill of raw, unadulterated terror that seemed to have crystallized in her bones.
Rex didn’t flinch at the cold; instead, his grip closed around hers like a vice warm, steady, and impossibly grounding.

She watched as his eyelids fluttered shut, and she witnessed something terrifying: the last vestige of the man who teased and laughed vanished, replaced by the flat, hollow stillness of a surgeon about to make the first incision.
His entire presence shifted into a focused vacuum, as if he had ceased to be a person and had become merely an instrument of the ritual.
The candle flame did not flicker.
It didn’t dance or sway as if caught in a breeze.
Instead, the physics of the room simply seemed to fail.
The light began to bend unnaturally, stretching thin and pale, warping toward a point in space that shouldn’t exist.
The flame took on a sickly, ethereal quality, a color that defied description, something caught halfway between a dead man’s blue and a tarnished silver.
Iris felt the air around them thicken.
The atmospheric pressure dropped so suddenly her ears popped painfully, and a heavy, charged sensation settled over her skin, like the moments before a catastrophic lightning strike.
The space was being violently reorganized around a purpose it had never held before.
"I have it," Rex said.
His voice was barely a whisper, stripped of all emotion, vibrating not from his throat but from somewhere deeper in his chest.
His eyes remained closed, his jaw set in stone.
"The thread is there... twenty-six days old, exactly as I told you it would be..."
"The temporal residue is still clinging to the ether like blood on a blade."
A bead of sweat rolled down Iris’s temple, but she didn’t dare move.
Her inner voice screamed at her to run, to flee this cursed room before whatever he summoned tore her apart, but she remained frozen.
"I am going to reach for it now," Rex continued, his grip tightening on her hands until it was almost painful.
"This part may take a moment."
"The tether is stubborn...
It will resist being pulled back into the light." Rex gritted his teeth.
"Iris, listen to me... do not let go of my hands."
"No matter what you see, no matter how much your mind screams that it is impossible or wrong, do not break contact..." Rex closed his eyes.
"Whatever you see, stay here with me."
Iris managed a sharp, jerky nod, though she knew he couldn’t see it.
She squeezed his hands so hard her own fingers began to ache, anchoring herself to his physical warmth as the room’s light died away.
The strange, pale glow of the candle became the only thing left in existence, casting long, distorted shadows that seemed to writhe independently of the flame.
Then, in the space above and slightly behind Rex’s head, something began to manifest.
It did not arrive with a crash or a flash of light.
There was no thunderous proclamation of its return.
Instead, it bled into reality.
It arrived the way a figure emerges from a suffocating fog: first the edges, then the suggestion of form.
A shoulder materialized out of the gloom; the vague outline of a jawline appeared.
Then, slowly, painfully, as if the universe itself were reluctant to allow it, color began to seep back into the void.
The grayscale haze bled into flesh tones, into the fabric of clothing, and into the unmistakable texture of human existence.
Iris felt her breath catch in her throat, trapped behind a wall of rising panic.
Her heart hammered against her ribs with such violence she feared it would crack them.
The fog resolved, the edges sharpened, and the silhouette solidified into something so familiar, so achingly real, that the recognition hit her like a physical blow to the solar plexus.
The ghost of her past was no longer a memory; he was standing three feet away, solid and breathing, emerging from the silver fire of Rex’s magic.
It Was Veylor...

chapters.title: Chapter 963. I Held The Bridge Between Life And Death, My Hands Bled
paragraphs: Veylor stood at the bleeding edge of the candlelight. He was translucent, his form faintly luminous like moonlight trapped in water, wearing the same simple, travel-worn field clothes he had been clad in the last time Iris had seen him breathing.

He looked impossibly fragile, yet he possessed a terrifying solidity that defied the laws of nature. The moment his pale and luminous eyes found hers, his entire expression shattered. His face broke open with a raw, naked disbelief so profound it acted like a sledgehammer against Iris’s carefully constructed emotional defenses.
"Iris," he said.

The sound of his voice transmitted a physical shockwave to her. It didn’t sound like a normal human voice; it was layered, echoing as though it were arriving from a vast distance while simultaneously vibrating inside her own skull.
It was the sound of a memory trying to become flesh again.
"I am here," Iris gasped.

Her voice was a wreck, a broken thing that betrayed every lie she had told herself over the last thirty-six days. The careful, rigid control she had maintained, the armor she had forged from grief and stubbornness, dissolved instantly.
Her hands trembled violently in Rex’s grip, and she felt a sob clawing at the back of her throat.
Veylor took a tentative step forward. As he moved, the light around him didn’t just bend; it rippled, distorting the air as if he were walking through deep water.
He wasn’t truly bound by the room’s physical space; he was choosing to manifest within it, forcing his ghostly essence into a shape that the world could recognize.
"I did not think I would see you again," Veylor whispered, his gaze raking over her face with desperate hunger. "I remember... I remember the fall, Iris."
"I remember the wind screaming past my ears and the ground rushing up so fast, so impossibly fast..."

"I remember the impact, that horrible, wet crack of bone, the taste of copper in my mouth as my lungs collapsed..." His voice wavered, his translucent fingers twitching as if feeling phantom pain. "And then there was nothing..."
"Just a vast, quiet grey place... No pain, no sound, no time."
"Just an endless, hollow emptiness. And now..." His eyes welled with something that looked like liquid silver. "...now I am here."
"I am standing before you, and I do not understand... I do not understand how the dead can speak."

Iris felt her heart breaking all over again, with each beat feeling like a fresh wound. She wanted to scream at him, to pull him into her arms and hold him until the universe corrected its mistake, but she knew the cost.
She knew the brutal mechanics of what Rex was doing.
"It is not going to last, Veylor," she said, her voice cracking on his name.
She forced herself to meet his luminous gaze, fighting the urge to collapse. "This isn’t a resurrection... This is a working soul thing... A temporary bridge built across the abyss."
She swallowed hard, the metallic taste of terror in her mouth. "One conversation..."
"That is all this ritual allows, and that is the price of breaking the veil.
"I knew the cost when I asked Rex to do this... I knew I would have to say goodbye again, immediately after saying hello."
"But I decided I wanted this anyway... I needed to hear your voice more than I needed to stay sane."

Veylor’s translucent face shifted, the luminous features contorting through something that looked, even in the eerie, silvered light of the ritual, unmistakably like raw, unvarnished grief. The spectral glow of his skin seemed to pulse in rhythm with his anguish.
"One conversation," he repeated, the words hollow and echoing. "After everything we were... After everything we promised."
"Just one conversation."
"I know," Iris choked out, the words feeling like shards of glass in her throat. "I am sorry, Veylor..."

"I am so sorry it couldn’t be more... I couldn’t save you... I watched Tremor... I watched that monster crush the life out of you while I stood there paralyzed, and I am sorry that I couldn’t give you more than this stolen moment..."
"Do not apologize," Veylor snapped.

His voice cracked violently, the specific, devastating fracture of someone who had been holding a fragile dam together only to feel it shatter completely. "Don’t you dare apologize to me for being here at all, Iris!"
He took a step closer, his form flickering as if the effort to maintain his presence was draining his very essence. "I have thought about you every single day since the fall..."
"Since that moment on the battlefield when the sky turned red and the earth shook under Tremor’s boots..."
"In whatever that grey place actually was—if ’thinking’ is even the right word for the consciousness that exists in that void—I thought about you."
His ghostly eyes burned with a desperate intensity. "I thought about the western cliffs..."
"I thought about the way the wind sounds through the pines... and I thought about you standing in my doorway the morning before the expedition, your hair messy, telling me to come back in one piece."
"And I didn’t, Iris... I didn’t come back this time from Tremor..." Veylor’s face looked in pain. "I failed the only promise that actually mattered."

Tears were streaming down Iris’s face now, hot and relentless. She made no attempt to wipe them away; she simply let them fall, each droplet feeling like a physical manifestation of her thirty-six days of torment.
Her grip on Rex’s hands tightened to the point of agony, her fingernails digging into his skin. Rex remained unnaturally still, his jaw clenched so hard the muscles stood out like cords.

He was a statue of concentration, his entire being focused on anchoring this impossible bridge between life and death. Iris could feel the strain coming off him in waves; the magical feedback of holding a dead soul against the pull of the grave was clearly taking a brutal toll on his own spiritual reserves.
"You did not break a promise," Iris said, her voice gaining a fierce, desperate strength. "You died doing something you chose to do..."
"You died protecting people who couldn’t protect themselves..."
"You died fighting a monster so others could live... I have made peace with that part, Veylor." Iris smiled. "I have fought through the guilt and the rage to find that peace...
"I want you to know that before anything else: I am not angry at you for dying... I was never angry at you for that."

Veylor’s form flickered dangerously, his edges blurring as the candle flame sputtered. A look of profound confusion crossed his luminous features, a question that seemed too heavy for even a ghost to carry.
"Then what," Veylor asked, his voice dropping to a haunting whisper that seemed to vibrate through Iris’s very bones. "If you have made peace with my death... what is the conversation you needed?"
"What could possibly be worth breaking the laws of heaven and hell for, if not that?"

Iris took a breath, a ragged, unsteady thing that rattled in her chest like broken glass. It was the breath of someone standing on the edge of a precipice, about to speak words she had rehearsed in the dead of night until they bled into her subconscious, only to find that the reality of the moment made them nearly impossible to articulate.
The air in the room felt charged with a static fury, the magical tether between Rex, Iris, and Veylor pulling taut like a bowstring ready to snap.
"I need to let you go," she said.
The words were quiet, but they cut through the supernatural silence of the room with devastating precision. "I need to do it properly, Veylor..."
"Not just in the sense that you are already gone, not in the physical sense but in the sense that I need to release you from the memory of me."
Veylor flinched as if she had struck him. His translucent form wavered violently, his edges blurring into the shadows.
"These last thirty-six days..." Iris continued, her voice gaining a desperate, painful momentum. "I have been carrying you around like something unfinished..."
"Like a conversation that was severed mid-sentence by a blade... I have been hoarding your memory like a sacred relic, but it has become a cage."

"I cannot keep living as though we are still together when there is no you here to hold, no you here to argue with, and no you here to simply be..." Iris dropped a single tear. "It is not fair to me, Veylor."
"And God help me, it is not fair to you too... I refuse to let you exist as nothing more than a wound that refuses to close."
"I refuse to let you be defined by the way you died."

Veylor stared at her, his luminous eyes fixed on hers with an intensity that felt like it could burn through her skin. His face went unnaturally still, the silver light fading from his features to something colder and more hollow.
"You are... ending it...?" he said.

His voice was stripped of its earlier desperation, leaving behind something raw and terrifyingly empty. "You summoned me from the abyss; you tore through the veil of reality with Rex’s blood and magic, just to... to say goodbye...?"
"You used our one chance to speak to deliver a eulogy?"
"Yes!" Iris cried out, her voice finally breaking properly, the sound tearing from her throat in a sob she could no longer contain. "Because I cannot breathe without saying it!"
"I loved you, Veylor! Do you hear me? I loved you with everything I was, and I will love you until my own heart stops beating."
"That truth isn’t going anywhere... It isn’t going to stop being true just because I am saying goodbye."

chapters.title: Chapter 964. I Am Bleeding Into Your Palms, The Price Of Honesty
paragraphs: She leaned forward, her forehead nearly touching his ghostly image, though she knew she would only feel the biting chill of his displaced existence. "But you are gone..."
"You have been gone for twenty-six days, and I have spent every single one of those days pretending... In some quiet, rotting corner of my soul, I have been waiting."
"I have been pretending that some part of you was still standing behind me, watching over me, waiting for me to catch up to you... And that pretense is killing me."
Her fingernails dug into Rex’s palms so hard she felt the wet heat of blood beginning to seep between their joined hands; the price of the ritual was becoming physical, brutal.
"I need to move on, Veylor," she whispered, her tears dripping onto the floor like molten silver in the candlelight. "I need to actually allow myself to live again..."
"And I cannot do that while I am still holding onto a ghost..." Iris shook her head. "I cannot build a future while I am still shackled to a corpse."
"I need to let you go... for both of us... and the greater good."
The silence that followed Iris’s confession was absolute, a suffocating weight that seemed to press the very oxygen from the room.

It stretched long enough that panic began to claw at her throat. She wondered if the working had catastrophically failed, if the connection had severed mid-sentence, leaving Veylor to dissolve back into the formless fog of the abyss without the closure she so desperately craved.
Then, from where he knelt like a living statue, his eyes still closed and his grip on her hands unyielding despite the visible strain in his tendons, Rex began to laugh.

It wasn’t a cruel laugh, nor was it mocking. It was the low, rumbling amusement of a man who had witnessed the universe conspire to make a moment of profound tragedy swing violently into the realm of the absurd.

The sound was jarring against the backdrop of Iris’s raw grief. She turned to glare at him, her eyes red rimmed and furious even through the tears, but the expression died halfway when she saw Veylor’s translucent form actually blink.

The ghost looked genuinely startled, the specific expression of a dead man who had expected a celestial reunion but found himself caught in the middle of a domestic argument anchored by a laughing necromancer.
"You couldn’t have led with something gentler, could you?" Rex said, his voice rough but warm.

He still didn’t open his eyes; he couldn’t. The magical feedback would shatter his concentration, but his shoulders shook with the effort of containing the mirth. "You waited twenty-six days of agonizing torment for one single conversation, and the very first thing out of your mouth is breaking up with a dead man."
"I did not plan it to sound like that!" Iris snapped, her mortification rising like bile.
She wiped at her face with the back of her wrist, smearing tears and salt across her cheeks. "I meant it kindly, Rex! I meant it as an act of mercy!"
"I understood the kindness underneath the brutality, Iris," Veylor said. Despite the ethereal glow of his skin, there was a new softness in his expression.
A small, unsteady laugh of his own escaped him, a broken, haunting sound that seemed to vibrate in the space between them. "You have never once in your life said anything gently..."
"You approach everything like a siege, and that’s why I loved that about you.
"I’m not going to pretend I’m surprised that even a supernatural visitation came out sounding like an assassin’s report rather than a farewell."
"I am trying, Veylor," Iris whispered.

She was caught in that terrible, honest limbo where laughter and sobbing become indistinguishable, two opposing forces tangled together in her chest until she couldn’t tell which one was winning. "I am trying so hard to do this right."
"I know you are," Veylor said.

The warmth in his voice was undeniable, undiminished by the crushing grief that still sat like lead in his ghostly chest. His form flickered brighter for a moment, a surge of recognition passing between them.
"And I am not angry... I want you to hear that as clearly as you wanted me to hear the rest of it."
"I am not hurt by your honesty."
He leaned forward as far as his spectral nature would allow, his luminous eyes searching hers. "You deserve to move on, Iris."
"You deserve to let someone hold you, someone who has bones you can touch, someone who can actually answer your touch with heat instead of this cold light..."

"I have thought about very little else in that grey place except how much I wanted exactly that for you... Even while some smaller, uglier part of me, the part that still belongs to you, hated the very idea of it."

Veylor’s form flickered violently, his edges fraying like burnt parchment. The instability was terrifying to witness the raw, metaphysical strain of a soul being forced into a shape it was never meant to hold for this long.

The luminous silver of his skin began to pulse erratically, each pulse accompanied by a low, harmonic hum that made Iris’s teeth ache. His expression shifted, the resigned acceptance dissolving into something far more primal: desperation.
It was a raw, grasping quality, the look of a drowning man reaching for a lifeline that was already slipping through his fingers.
"Is there truly no other way?" he asked.

His voice had lost its melodic echo; it was now thin, strained, as if he were speaking through a throat filled with ash. He wasn’t looking at Iris anymore; he was looking past her, his luminous gaze fixed on Rex with a pleading intensity.
"There must be some loophole... Some crack in the foundation."
"Tell me there is a way to keep some thread between us, Rex...! A dream, once a year?! A sign in the wind she would recognize as mine?!"
"A bird that flies wrong, a shadow that lingers too long?"
Veylor’s form convulsed, a spark of static energy jumping from his shoulder to the floor. "I do not need to be here like this.
"I do not need flesh and bone and this terrible, borrowed solidity... I only need to know there is some door left open... Even if it’s a crack or even... a door that opens only once in a lifetime."
"Just... don’t tell me I’m truly erased."
The tension in the room reached a breaking point. Iris could feel the magical pressure building, a physical weight pressing against her chest like a stone.
She could hear Rex’s breathing, heavy and ragged, each exhale sounding like grinding metal as he fought to maintain the ritual’s integrity against the encroaching void.
Then, Rex opened his eyes.
They were bloodshot, the whites mapped with crimson veins from the sheer strain of the necromantic channeling. The pale, unnatural light of the workshop reflected in his pupils like twin dying stars.

When he spoke, the sound wasn’t comforting. It carried the specific, unshakeable finality of a judge passing sentence, the voice of a man who had already mapped every possible outcome, weighed every cosmic variable, and found no salvation.
"There is no door, Veylor," Rex said.
His voice was gentle, but it was a gentleness that offered no shelter from the truth. "I am not here to give you false hope to soften the blow."
"That would be a cruelty worse than the truth itself."
Rex’s knuckles were white where they gripped Iris’s hands, and Iris could feel the heat of his blood where the magical feedback was beginning to tear at his own capillaries.

"The working I used to pull you across the veil draws on a connection that only exists because the thread between you and Iris has not yet completed its transition," Rex explained, each word measured and precise, though his jaw was clenched so tight it looked ready to shatter. "You are still tethered to her by the unfinished business of your grief and her refusal to let go."
"This ritual isn’t creating something new... it is exploiting the wound you left behind."
"But once this conversation ends, once she says what she needs to say and truly releases you, that wound will begin to scar..."
"The thread will finish what it was always going to finish: it will sever."
Rex’s gaze locked onto Veylor’s fading form, unflinching. "There will be no dreams, Veylor."
"No signs in the wind... No whispers in the night... and what is happening right now is not a glimpse through a window."
"This moment is the door. And it is closing the very instant I release the work."

"But you are gone..."
"You have been gone for twenty-six days, and I have spent every single one of those days pretending...
In some quiet, rotting corner of my soul, I have been waiting."
"I have been pretending that some part of you was still standing behind me, watching over me, waiting for me to catch up to you...
And that pretense is killing me."
Her fingernails dug into Rex’s palms so hard she felt the wet heat of blood beginning to seep between their joined hands; the price of the ritual was becoming physical, brutal.
"I need to move on, Veylor," she whispered, her tears dripping onto the floor like molten silver in the candlelight.
"I need to actually allow myself to live again..."
"And I cannot do that while I am still holding onto a ghost..." Iris shook her head.
"I cannot build a future while I am still shackled to a corpse."
"I need to let you go... for both of us... and the greater good."
The silence that followed Iris’s confession was absolute, a suffocating weight that seemed to press the very oxygen from the room.
It stretched long enough that panic began to claw at her throat.

She wondered if the working had catastrophically failed, if the connection had severed mid-sentence, leaving Veylor to dissolve back into the formless fog of the abyss without the closure she so desperately craved.

It was the low, rumbling amusement of a man who had witnessed the universe conspire to make a moment of profound tragedy swing violently into the realm of the absurd.
The sound was jarring against the backdrop of Iris’s raw grief.
She turned to glare at him, her eyes red rimmed and furious even through the tears, but the expression died halfway when she saw Veylor’s translucent form actually blink.

The ghost looked genuinely startled, the specific expression of a dead man who had expected a celestial reunion but found himself caught in the middle of a domestic argument anchored by a laughing necromancer.
"You couldn’t have led with something gentler, could you?" Rex said, his voice rough but warm.

The magical feedback would shatter his concentration, but his shoulders shook with the effort of containing the mirth.

chapters.title: Chapter 965. It’s Finally Time To Stop Acting Gentle... And Show My True Face!
paragraphs: Veylor’s translucent features didn’t just fall; they crumbled. It was the specific, devastating collapse of a soul hearing a truth that had no mercy and no exceptions, the kind of certainty that makes the universe feel suddenly, terrifyingly small.
The silver light that composed his body flickered like a candle caught in a death wind, casting jagged, dancing shadows across the room.
"Then let me have a moment longer," he whispered.
His voice was no longer the melodic echo of a spirit; it was thick, raw, and human in its desperation. "Please... I am not asking for a future."

"And I am not asking for a miracle as well, but just... let me look at her. Properly." A shudder ran through his spectral frame, sending ripples through his form like stone dropped in still water. "I didn’t get to look at her last time..."
"Everything moved too fast: the steel, the blood, the screaming... I want this to be the last thing I carry."
"I want this image to be the only thing that remains when I slip into whatever comes after this... If there even is an after."

Rex remained silent, but the cost of his silence—Rex’s silence—spoke volumes, evident in the violent strain of his body. Iris could feel the tremor running through him; his grip on her hands tightened instinctively, knuckles grinding against each other.

She could hear the wet, labored sound of his breathing, the sound of a man pushing his own life force through a needle’s eye. His jaw was set so hard she feared she might hear his teeth crack under the pressure of maintaining the necromantic tether.
He was fighting the very laws of reality to keep this door from slamming shut prematurely.
"You have it," Rex gritted out through clenched teeth, his voice strained by the effort of holding the magical current steady. "As long as I can keep the thread from snapping."
"Take the time, Veylor... I am not going anywhere."
Veylor turned his gaze fully toward Iris, and Iris turned hers toward him. For a long, suspended moment, the world outside the circle ceased to exist.
There was no ritual, no necromancy, no bleeding necromancer; there was only the devastating silence of two people existing in the same space for one final, stolen heartbeat.

It was a communication beyond language, a silent collision of memories, shared touches, and the hollow ache of what had been severed. They simply were, two halves of a broken whole, staring across the impossible divide between life and death.
Then, Iris made her choice.
Without releasing Rex’s blood-slicked hands, she shifted, turning her body toward the living man. She pressed herself against Rex’s side, seeking the solidity of his heat, the reality of his pulse.

She buried her face against his shoulder, inhaling the salt of his sweat and the metallic tang of the ritual’s blood. Rex didn’t falter; despite the agony of the work demanding his absolute focus, his arm came around her, pulling her close, anchoring her to the earth while she faced the sky.
Iris lifted her head slightly, her eyes locking onto Veylor’s luminous gaze one last time. Her voice was thick with unshed tears, but the waver was gone.
The breaking had finished. What remained was something tempered, something forged in the fire of her grief.
"He is who I love now," Iris said, the words quiet but carrying the weight of an unbreakable vow.
She spoke directly to Veylor, offering him the truth as a final gift: the truth of her survival. "I want you to see that too, before you go..."
"I want you to know that I am not walking away from this conversation into some empty void... I am not walking into nothingness either."
She tightened her hold on Rex, grounding herself in the present. "I am walking into something real, Veylor... I am walking into a life."
The admission hit Veylor with more violence than any blade could have. His entire spectral form convulsed, the silver light turning a sickly, bruised violet before flashing white.

For a moment, he couldn’t speak; he could only stare at the way Iris clung to Rex, the way her body instinctively sought the heat and strength of the necromancer. The shock was absolute, a metaphysical earthquake that seemed to crack the very air around them.
"You... you can’t mean that," Veylor stammered, his voice rising in pitch, cracking like breaking ice. "Iris, no...! "That’s—that’s not you!"
"That’s the grief talking! That’s the trauma clinging to the first solid thing it found! You can’t replace what we—"
"I’m not replacing anything, Veylor," Iris interrupted, her voice muffled against Rex’s shoulder, but her words cutting through his panic like a scalpel. "I’m simply choosing to live."
"You’re choosing a monster!" Veylor screamed, the sound tearing from his throat in a raw, inhuman wail that made the candles gutter and die. "Iris, look at him!"
"Look at what he’s doing to you! He’s using you as an anchor, a battery for his filthy necromancy!"
"He doesn’t love you; he’s consuming you!"
At that moment, the atmosphere in the room shifted. The fragile, solemn sanctity of the farewell evaporated, replaced by something far more predatory.

Rex’s shoulders relaxed, but it wasn’t the relaxation of relief; it was the casual slouch of a predator who had finished playing with his food. The bloodshot eyes, once strained with effort, suddenly cleared, revealing pupils that burned with a cold, calculating malice.
His gentle mask didn’t just slip; it shattered, revealing the grinning villain beneath.
"Oh, let him scream, Iris," Rex said, his voice dropping to a smooth, terrifying purr.
He didn’t look at Veylor; he kept his eyes on Iris, savoring the way she shuddered against him. "Let him play his part..."
’It’s adorable, really... The ghost trying to protect a woman who has already surrendered her soul to someone far more interesting."
Rex turned his head slightly to acknowledge Veylor, a cruel, mocking smile twisting his lips. "Rest assured, little ghost.
"She is in excellent hands. Better than yours, certainly." Rex laughed. "I don’t just hold her heart; I own the very rhythm of it."
"I don’t offer her dreams; I offer her reality... It’s a harsh, bleeding, and beautiful reality, to be exact."
"You... you bastard!" Veylor lunged forward, his hands outstretched as if he could physically tear Iris away from the necromancer. "I will destroy you! I will--"
"You will do nothing," Rex interrupted, his tone turning glacial. "Because you aren’t going anywhere."
Rex’s grip on Iris’s waist tightened painfully, his fingers digging into her flesh. "Iris, darling, you’re getting so worked up."
"Can you feel it?" His voice became a hypnotic murmur. "The way your heart races when I touch you like this?"
"The way your body betrays your pretty little words?"

As Rex tapped into the full, unholy potential of his soul manipulation, the room exploded in sensory overload. The air became thick with the smell of burnt copper and something sweeter, something almost cloying: the scent of raw spiritual energy.
A low, thrumming vibration shook the floorboards, a sound that felt less like noise and more like a heartbeat pulsing through the bones of everyone present.

Iris let out a sharp, involuntary cry halfway between a sob and a moan as Rex’s power flooded her system. It wasn’t gentle. It was invasive. His magic crawled under her skin like liquid fire, claiming every nerve ending.
"Rex... please... it’s too much..." she gasped, her head rolling back, her eyes fluttering.

The pleasure and pain were so intertwined she couldn’t distinguish between them; her body arched against his, a desperate, involuntary response to the overwhelming stimulation of his necromantic touch.
"It’s exactly enough," Rex whispered against her ear, his breath hot and mocking.
With a guttural incantation that sounded like bones grinding together, Rex unleashed a shockwave of pure soul force. "You wanted to stay, Veylor? Fine... Stay as long as you want before you go back."

The silver light that made up Veylor’s form was suddenly seized by invisible chains of black ichor. Veylor’s scream became a prolonged, agonized shriek as the magic tore into his essence, not to destroy him, but to bind him.

He was slammed backward against the far wall, his form pinned there by crushing gravitational force. The magic didn’t just trap his body; it trapped his consciousness, forcing him to remain conscious and watch.

"I want you to witness this," Rex said, his eyes glowing with a hellish intensity as he watched Veylor struggle against the invisible bonds. "I want you to see exactly what happens when a ghost tries to interfere with a god."
"You wanted to watch her? Fine... Watch how she belongs to me."

The room echoed with a terrifying chorus: Veylor’s desperate, impotent screams of rage; the wet, rhythmic sounds of Rex’s magic working through Iris’s body; and Iris’s own broken, high, keening moans that tore through the air as she drowned in the overwhelming, terrifying ecstasy of being completely, utterly consumed by the man who had stolen her life and replaced it with something far more dangerous.

chapters.title: Chapter 966. I’m Going To Completely Ruin Iris While His Ghost Boyfriend Watches...**
paragraphs: The room became a theater of the obscene, the air thick with the copper tang of blood and the cloying, musky sweetness of unleashed desire. Rex stood in the center of the ritual circle, a predator who had finally cornered his prey, his eyes burning with a dark, unholy triumph.
With a casual flick of his wrist, his telekinetic power lashed out like invisible whips, wrapping around Veylor’s spectral throat and limbs.
The ghost was slammed against the wall with such force that his form rippled like disturbed water, pinned there by chains of pure necrotic force that severed his ability to make any sound.
Veylor could scream until his very essence shattered, but no sound would escape his lips; he was a prisoner of silence, forced to witness everything through a lens of helpless terror.
"Now then," Rex purred, his voice cutting through the low hum of magical energy. "Let’s remove these unnecessary barriers."
With obscene ease, Rex began to undress. His movements were slow, deliberate, and dripping with menace.

His telekinesis stripped away his own clothes as if they were nothing more than autumn leaves, revealing a body that was a temple of scarred muscle and corded sinew. His tan skin glistened under the flickering candlelight, each muscle defined by the sweat of the working.
As he stood bare, his cock massive, veined, and already weeping with pre-cum, it hung heavy between his thighs, a weapon of flesh waiting to be deployed.
He turned his attention to Iris. "And you, my darling..."
"You’ve been waiting for this, haven’t you? Don’t lie to me."

Iris was trembling violently, her body caught in a vicious cycle of terror and arousal. Her mind screamed at her to flee, to reject this violation, but Rex’s soul manipulation had already rewritten her nervous system.

She clung to the rationalizations like a drowning woman to driftwood. She told herself the sleeplessness was the price of discipline, the relentless administrative burden of managing a son who had become a volatile variable in her carefully ordered world.
She checked his meals with obsessive precision; she monitored his movements with the cold calculation of a warden.

A guard now stood silently outside his door, not as a punishment, but as a necessary barrier between Theo’s fractured psyche and the rest of the world. She convinced herself that this vigilance was her duty, a necessary tax paid for the preservation of order.
But deep down, in the hollow spaces where her conscience resided, she knew she was lying. The sleeplessness wasn’t vigilance; it was terror.
The household was still draped in the grey, pre-dawn silence when she began crossing the rear corridor toward the kitchens. The air was cold, smelling of old stone and extinguished beeswax.
Her footsteps were muffled, ghostly echoes against the flagstones. She was moving earlier than any servant would expect, seeking the solitary comfort of routine.
Then, the silence shattered.
Theo’s door swung open with a violence that reverberated through the narrow stone passage. The crash of wood against stone sounded like a gunshot.
Aurelia’s body reacted before her mind could process the sound; her fingers instinctively flew to the hilt of the dagger strapped to her hip, her knuckles whitening as she prepared to draw.
Her heart hammered against her ribs like a trapped bird, adrenaline flooding her system, sharpening the edges of her vision.

Theo stood framed in the doorway, a silhouette of chaos against the dim light of his room. He was still wearing yesterday’s clothes, now wrinkled and stained, clinging to his frame like a second, diseased skin.

His hair was a matted thicket, disordered from restless tossing, but it was his eyes that stopped her breath. They were bloodshot, pupils blown wide with a wild, unslept quality that screamed of mania and exhaustion.
There was something primal in his gaze, something that suggested the boy she knew had been replaced by something hollowed out and dangerous.
A cold dread pooled in her stomach, heavy as lead. Her mind raced through possibilities.

Aurelia’s fury ignited instantly, a searing, white-hot flash that burned through the fog of her exhaustion. It was the reflexive, defensive anger of a woman who had been hollowed out by days of damage control, managing the catastrophic fallout of her son’s previous unraveling.
Her patience wasn’t just thin; it was gone, incinerated by the relentless stress of maintaining a facade of control while her world crumbled.

"You are supposed to be confined to this room," she hissed, her voice dropping to a dangerous, razor-edged register that promised pain. "You do not get to simply breach your confinement because you decided you had something to say!"
"You have forfeited the right to speak without permission!"
"I know!" Theo exploded, the sound raw and ugly.
He took a stumbling step toward her, his hands shaking so violently they looked like blurred shadows. "I know I shouldn’t be here..."
"I know I’ve fucked up, I know I’ve disappointed you, and I know you want to throw me back in that cell and bolt the door!"
"But none of that matters right now... none of it compares to what I need you to hear." His eyes searched hers with a terrifying intensity. "Please... Just this once."
"For the love of whatever gods are left, listen before you punish me for what I’m about to say."

Something in the sheer, unvarnished desperation of his voice struck a nerve in Aurelia. It was a primal frequency; she recognized the specific, reluctant pause of a mother who had spent three decades learning to distinguish between her son performing a tantrum and her son experiencing a genuine psychological collapse.
This wasn’t defiance; this was a man drowning.
"Speak," she commanded, though her grip on the dagger loosened fractionally. "Quickly, and quietly, before the household wakes and finds you standing outside a door you are not permitted to touch."
"Choose your words carefully, Theo... Your next breath could be your last."
Theo took a breath, but it didn’t steady him. It came out as a shuddering, broken gasp that rattled in his chest.
His mind was screaming, a cacophony of images that refused to dim. ’I saw it... I saw the truth behind the mask. ’
’I saw the monster beneath the mentor.’
"I saw something," he began, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper that carried more weight than a scream. "Last night and the night before that in whatever passes for sleep now.
"It’s not sleep, Mother... It’s a liminal hell where my mind goes when my body finally collapses from exhaustion."
’I saw Rex."
Aurelia stiffened, her entire body going rigid. "Rex has nothing to do with--"
"You don’t understand!" Theo interrupted, his words tumbling out in a desperate, unstoppable torrent. "I saw him! But not as the man who trains with me!"
"I saw him yesterday...! Now, I fucking knew that he wasn’t human!" Theo clenched both his fists. "He was something ancient, something terrible!"

"He was the one all along...! The one who wears armor forged from living stone, and I saw the mask." His breathing became ragged, his eyes darting as if the memory were physically attacking him. "I saw him tearing this city apart with those same hands, the same hands that have been correcting my footwork, guiding my stance, and touching my shoulders in the training hall for the last two weeks!"
"Those hands were slick with blood, Mother...! I saw the entrails spray against the cobblestones as he crushed them."
Aurelia went utterly still. The blood drained from her face, leaving her skin as pale as the stone walls surrounding them.
A cold sweat broke across her brow.
"He is Tremor," Theo said, the name hitting the air like a death sentence. "The Forbidden Earthen Apostle!"
"The butcher of the plaza... The monster responsible for the slaughter, the one who left half this city in ruins and half its people in graves!"
"I saw it as clearly as I am seeing your face right now!"
"I saw him reveal himself not to a stranger, but to Iris’s boyfriend, Tremor, when he showed his true form... I saw the connection."
He grabbed his own hair, twisting it as if trying to extract the memory from his skull. "I know how it sounds!"
"I know I’m the madman... and I know I’m the boy who lost his mind in the guest room, the boy who can’t be trusted!"
"But I am telling you the truth! Rex is the monster we’ve been hunting!"
"Theo," Aurelia said, her voice cracking with a warning weight that could have felled a lesser man. "Stop... Stop this instant."

She told herself the sleeplessness was the price of discipline, the relentless administrative burden of managing a son who had become a volatile variable in her carefully ordered world.

Her footsteps were muffled, ghostly echoes against the flagstones.

chapters.title: Chapter 981. Even After Saying All Of That... The Mother Didn’t Give Single Shits!
paragraphs: "There is more," Theo gasped, and the desperation in his eyes had curdled into something far more dangerous: a feverish, glassy-eyed mania.

His pupils were pinpricks of terror, his skin slick with a cold, sickly sweat that made him look like a corpse already beginning to decay. "I saw Iris... God help me, I saw what happened in her room yesterday."
Aurelia flinched as if he had struck her. "Theo, cease this at once--"
"I know I have no right!" he shrieked, the sound tearing from his throat like broken glass. "I know it isn’t my business; I know I should have been blind to it, but the vision didn’t ask permission!"
"It didn’t give me a choice before it tore open my mind and forced me to watch! And I saw enough to know... I saw enough to know that she is carrying his child now!"
The silence that followed was deafening, a physical pressure that seemed to suck the oxygen from the corridor.
"Rex has gotten Iris pregnant, Mother," Theo continued, his words coming faster now, spilling out in a torrent of horrified revelation. "He has infected this entire household like a plague!"

"He has everyone wrapped around his finger, twisted around his will without any of us understanding what he actually is beneath that practiced charm, those perfect training corrections, and that false, steady gaze that makes everyone believe he genuinely cares." His voice dropped to a horrified whisper. "And it was worse than that."
"He didn’t even hide it... He fucked her right there, right in front of her own boyfriend... Veylor! Yes! Veylor was there... watching as a ghost, powerless to stop it while Rex claimed her!"
The dam broke. Aurelia’s hand moved before her conscious mind could intervene: a sharp, vicious, open-palmed strike that cracked across Theo’s cheek with the sound of breaking bone.
The force of the blow sent him stumbling backward, his skull connecting painfully with the wooden doorframe of his own room.
"You would say anything," Aurelia hissed, her voice shaking with a fury that had transcended rage and become something raw, wounded, and utterly primal. "Anything at all, would you not?"

"Anything to poison this house, to make us doubt the one person who has done more for this family in two weeks than our own blood has managed in generations!" Her eyes burned with unshed tears of humiliation. "Do you hear the madness dripping from your tongue? Visions? Dreams?"
"You are describing the ravings of a broken boy who has already tried to murder two people in their sleep, and you expect me—you expect me to take a single word of this filth seriously?"
"I am not lying!" Theo roared back, the anguish in his voice so profound it felt like a physical wound in the air between them. "I know what it sounds like!"
"I know I sound like a monster, a liar, a madman!"
"But ask yourself honestly, Mother, look at the facts instead of your feelings! Has anything about Rex Rexilion ever truly added up?"
He took a step toward her despite the pain in his face, his hands clenched into white-knuckled fists. "The abilities that appeared out of thin air?!
"The intimate, impossible knowledge of the Underlayer that no ordinary student should possess?!"
"The convenient timing of every single rescue, every intervention, every disaster where he happens to materialize exactly when he is needed most?!"
"I am not asking you to trust a dream, Mother!"

"I am asking you to trust the pattern! The pattern that has been staring us in the face for months while we all pretended not to see it because looking at it meant questioning someone we had already decided to love!"
"Enough," Aurelia commanded, her voice cold as a tombstone, though her hands trembled uncontrollably.
"It is NOT enough!" Theo screamed, and something inside him finally shattered; the last tether to his composure snapped completely, leaving behind only grief, terror, and a drowning conviction.

"I am trying to save this family! I am trying to save you, and Iris, and Diana, from a man who has already stripped me bare and taken everything I own, and he is not going to stop simply because he has run out of things of mine left to take!"
A single tear tracked through the blood blooming on his cheek where he had struck the doorframe. "I tried to stop him the wrong way... I know that."
"I know what I did was unforgivable, and I am not asking for your forgiveness!"
"I am not asking for anything but this: Hear me... Just hear this one truth before it is too late for the rest of you the way it has already been too late for me!"
Aurelia stood paralyzed in the dim, flickering light of the corridor, her chest heaving as if she had been running. Her breathing came in ragged, wet gasps, each one echoing off the cold stone walls.

She stared at Theo, really stared at him, and what she saw made her stomach twist with a nauseating cocktail of horror, grief, and a rage so profound it felt like molten lead coursing through her veins.

"You broke something in yourself," she whispered finally. The words weren’t loud, but they carried the terrible, hollow weight of a funeral dirge. "That night in the guest room... that violence... it broke something fundamental."
"I told myself... I lied to myself that discipline and time would be enough to mend the cracks."
"I believed that if I held you tight enough, if I policed your every breath, I could stitch you back together." Her eyes glistened with a cruel, bitter moisture. "I see now how foolish I was..."
"What is standing in front of me right now... this thing speaking with your voice, wearing your face, using your memories to weaponize lies against us... it is not my son anymore.
"Mother, please—" Theo’s voice was a broken whimper, reaching for a connection that was rapidly evaporating.
"I am done listening, Theo." The words landed with the guillotine’s sharp finality of a closing tomb.
Before he could react, Aurelia lunged. Her fingers curled like talons into the fabric of his shirt, twisting the material until it threatened to tear.
She didn’t just hold him; she claimed him in a grip born of pure, unadulterated fury. Theo didn’t fight back.
He didn’t raise his hands to protect himself. He stood there with a terrifying, hollow acceptance, his shoulders slumped as if he were already a corpse waiting for the earth to claim him.
He believed he deserved the pain. He believed he earned every ounce of the torment she was about to unleash.
CRACK.

Her fist collided with his jaw with a wet, splintering sound that reverberated through the narrow passage. Theo’s head snapped sideways, blood immediately blooming from where his teeth had punched through the inside of his cheek.
He didn’t cry out; he simply absorbed the impact, his body swaying like a blade of grass in a storm.

"You are going to stand there," Aurelia hissed, her face inches from his, her breath hot against his skin as she struck him again, a vicious, closed fist blow that sent a spray of crimson droplets across the grey stone floor.
"You are going to stand there and accuse the man who saved this household of being a monster."
"The man who saved your worthless life more than once, who showed you more patience and mercy than you have ever shown yourself."

She struck him a third time, a brutal hook that forced a pained, gurgling sound from his throat. "You stand there and accuse him of corrupting Iris, a grown woman, a woman capable of her own desires and her own choices, as though she were some helpless child who cannot be trusted to know her own heart."
Her voice rose to a crescendo of controlled madness, her eyes wide and unblinking. "And you expect me to believe you?"
"You expect me to believe that this torrent of filth is coming from a place of clarity? No."
Her grip tightened until her knuckles turned white, her nails digging into his chest through the fabric. "This is not truth, Theo."
"This is not revelation... This is the bitter, poisoned madness of a man who cannot accept that he lost."
"This is the pathetic, self-destructive tantrum of a boy who would rather burn his entire world to ash than admit he was defeated by a better man."

chapters.title: Chapter 982. He Won The Moment You Chose A Sword Over Your Pride
paragraphs: The third strike was not merely a blow; it was a release of pent-up years of disappointment, a thunderclap of physical condemnation. The impact sounded like wet leather slapping stone, sending a spray of blood from Theo’s split lip across the wall. His legs buckled, but Aurelia was relentless.

She didn’t let him fall; she dragged him. Her fingers locked into the collar of his shirt like iron bands, her knuckles white and bloodless as she hauled his stumbling, broken form backward into the confines of his room.
The doorframe scraped against his shoulder with a sickening grinding noise as she shoved him inside. With a final, guttural snarl of disgust, she threw him.

Theo crashed onto the hardwood floor beside his bed with a bone-jarring thud that seemed to vibrate through the very foundations of the house. He lay there, curled on his side, gasping for air that tasted of copper and bile.
Aurelia stood over him, silhouetted against the dim light of the corridor, her chest heaving in violent, arrhythmic spasms. Her shadow loomed over him like a vengeful deity.

"I loved you enough to forgive the street," she began, her voice dropping to a low, terrifying register that made the hair on Theo’s neck stand on end. "I loved you enough to forgive the blood you spilled in those alleys, the chaos you sowed."

"I loved you enough to forgive the blade you turned on innocent people... God help me, I still do not know if that forgiveness was earned, or if I simply gave it because the alternative—the alternative of admitting my own son was a monster—was more than I could bear to face."
She took a step closer, the hem of her gown whispering against the floor like a serpent in the grass. "I do not know how much more of you I have left to forgive, Theo."
"I have given until there is nothing left in my own heart but scars. And I am beginning to be terrified that the answer is none..."
"That there is nothing left inside that hollow shell of yours worth the effort of saving... That you have finally become the void you always feared."
"Mother..." Theo croaked from the floor. The fire had gone out of him.

The manic conviction that had fueled his screaming was gone, replaced by a raw, childlike vulnerability that made him look smaller than he ever had. Blood leaked from the corner of his mouth, dripping steadily onto the floorboards.
"Mother, please... you have to... you have to believe me... Please."

Aurelia looked down at him, and for a moment, the mask of fury shattered. Beneath the rage, something cracked a fissure of grief so profound, so absolute, that it seemed to darken the very air between them.
It was the look of a woman watching something precious burn to ash in real time, knowing she was the one holding the torch.
"It is too late," she said, and the words were colder than any blade he had ever wielded. "Do you understand that, Theo?
"Truly understand?"
Her voice trembled with the weight of her final judgment. "It has been too late since the moment you raised that blade over their bed."
’Since the moment you chose violence over truth... You speak of conspiracies, of visions, of Rex Rexilion being some ancient demon."
"But you are wrong."
She leaned down, her face inches from his pain-streaked features, her eyes twin pools of frozen sorrow. "Rex has already won, Theo. "
"Not because of some grand scheme. Not because of some mystical prophecy that only your broken mind could perceive."
"He won because you handed him the crown... He won the moment you decided that your wounded pride was worth more than this family’s trust."
"You handed him victory the night you decided a sword was the answer to your own inadequacy."
She straightened up, pulling away from him as if his very presence contaminated her. "There is nothing left to fight for here."
"There is no enemy to vanquish, no monster to slay..."

"There is only the wreckage that remains to be managed. And I am the one who has to clean up the blood, because apparently no one else in this family is capable of stopping before the damage becomes permanent."
Aurelia retreated from his broken form, each step backward feeling like she was withdrawing from a battlefield where the enemy was her own blood.

She stopped at the threshold of the doorway, the shadow of the frame cutting across her face like a scar. The fire in her eyes had dimmed, leaving behind something far more devastating: the hollow, ashen glow of total exhaustion.
"This is my fault," she said.
The admission was quiet, almost fragile, but it carried more destructive power than all her screaming. It was the sound of a dam finally giving way.
"I should never have struck you that first time... Not in front of them. Not in front of the household."
She closed her eyes for a heartbeat, a shudder wracking her shoulders. "I told myself it was justice..."
"I told myself you deserved every blow for what you nearly did for the blood you almost spilled in that room.

"And perhaps you did deserve it. Perhaps every bruise you carry tonight is a debt paid." Her voice cracked, raw and bleeding. "But striking you did not fix whatever was already shattered inside you, Theo."
"It didn’t mend the cracks... All it did was confirm your darkest fears."
"It taught you that violence is the only language this family speaks when words fail..."
"I taught you that lesson, and you learned it with terrifying precision."

A single tear escaped her closed lids, tracking through the pale dust of her makeup. "Everything since then has simply been the two of us proving that lesson correct, over and over again, until there is nothing left between us but bruises, broken bones, and accusations that neither of us can ever take back."
"Then let me explain!" Theo screamed, the sound tearing from his lungs as he fought to push himself upright.

His muscles spasmed against the pain; his fingers scraped uselessly against the hardwood as he tried to haul his battered body off the floor. Blood smeared across the planks as he dragged himself up, his breathing a wet, desperate rattle.
"Mother, please! Just listen to the truth for just one minute of—"
"No."
The word was not a shout. It was a guillotine blade. It cut through his plea, severing his hope mid-sentence.
Aurelia reached for the handle and pulled the door shut. The click of the latch sounded like a gunshot in the sudden silence of the room.

Outside in the corridor, the household staff servants and guards who had gathered like carrion birds at the sound of the violence stood frozen. They watched with wide, terrified eyes as Aurelia turned the key in the lock from the outside, sealing her son in his own private hell.
Her hands were shaking so violently that the brass key rattled against the lock mechanism.
The fury was gone now. The rage had burned itself out, leaving behind nothing but the cold, dead embers of a mother who had lost everything.

She stood there for three seconds, a statue of grief in the dim hallway, before she turned her back on the door. She did not look at the staff. She did not acknowledge the whispered conversations or the frightened glances of those who witnessed her humiliation.
She simply walked away, her footsteps echoing down the hall like the steady, inevitable march of a funeral procession.

chapters.title: Chapter 983. Exhaustion Turns Certainties Into Shadows, She Was Living Proof
paragraphs: Rex found her in the training hall exactly one hour later. The space was cavernous, filled with the sharp tang of sweat and floor wax, lit only by the pale, sickly glow of the moon filtering through the high windows.

Aurelia was alone, a solitary figure caught in the rhythm of violence. She was running the same brutal conditioning drills he had run through himself the week before—drills designed to break a person before they were built.

Her movements were sharp, mechanical, and surgically controlled, but beneath that technical precision lurked something feral. Every strike against the heavy leather sandbag carried the echo of a scream; every pivot was too fast, too desperate, as if she were trying to outrun the ghost of her own choices.
Rex watched her from the arched doorway, his silhouette motionless. He didn’t speak immediately, letting the wet thwack of her fists against leather fill the silence.
He could see the way her muscles coiled and snapped, the way her knuckles were already beginning to split and weep crimson droplets onto the training mat.
"I heard," he said quietly as he finally crossed the floor, his boots making no sound against the reinforced wood.

Aurelia did not stop. She unleashed a devastating combination of a left hook, right cross, and spinning elbow; each strike was delivered with the specific, focused brutality of someone using physical agony to process an emotional wound that refused to clot.
The sandbag groaned under the assault.
"The entire household heard," she snapped, her voice ragged.
She didn’t turn. "I did not exactly manage the volume of it."

"I am not here to judge how you managed it," Rex said, stopping just outside her striking radius. His voice was steady, a calm anchor in the storm of her exertion. "I am here because you should not be doing this alone... Not tonight."
Aurelia stopped abruptly. Her chest heaved in violent, uncontrolled spasms, and her breath came in harsh, whistling gasps that tore at her throat.
Her knuckles were raw, the skin split and weeping blood that streaked down her wrists like macabre bracelets. She turned to face him fully, and the exhaustion that met his gaze was terrifying.
It wasn’t just physical fatigue; it was the hollow, sunken look of someone whose soul had been scraped raw.
"He accused you," she said, the words tumbling out like broken glass. "Of being Tremor."
"Of getting Iris pregnant." Her eyes searched his, desperate and accusatory. "He said it with such conviction, Rex."
"Such absolute, terrifying certainty..."
"For one terrible moment, standing there in that doorway while I held him down, while I struck him... I found myself actually wondering."
"The doubt felt like a blade between my ribs.
Rex didn’t flinch. He met her gaze with the careful, unnatural stillness of a man who had learned to weigh the gravity of every lie.
He studied her, calculating exactly how much pressure the truth could withstand before it shattered.
"And what did you decide?" he asked, his voice dropping to a low murmur.
"I decided he was broken," Aurelia said, though her voice wavered. "I told myself that in the night in that guest room, the blood, the blade—it broke something fundamental in him."
"That it created a fracture that hasn’t stopped spreading... I told myself that a broken man will reach for any narrative, any twisted story that lets him believe he was righteous in his madness."

"I decided that believing him would mean accepting that my son might have stumbled onto something true, and I decided I had to decide that I could not survive that thought while standing in the wreckage of my own home."
"You made the correct decision," Rex said firmly. His tone left no room for argument.
"Did I?" Aurelia whispered.
Something in her voice cracked, not with the fury she had shown Theo, but with an aching, poisonous uncertainty. "I do not know anymore, Rex..."
"I have struck my own son twice in one week."
"I have looked at him and told him he is unrecognizable. And perhaps that was fair... Perhaps he is unrecognizable."
She took a stumbling step toward him, her hands shaking, the blood from her knuckles smearing across her training gear. "But then there are the pieces that don’t fit... the abilities you possess."
"The knowledge you carry, the names, the places, the secrets of people you should have no way of knowing."
’I told him none of it added up to a conspiracy."

"I told him you were the exception, the miracle." Her eyes welled with tears she refused to let fall. "But I am standing here now, Rex, and I am less certain of that than I was when I was screaming in his face."
Rex closed the remaining distance between them, his movements deliberate and unhurried, like a predator approaching something fragile rather than something hostile.
He reached out and placed his hand against the leather-bound post beside her, the contact sending a dull vibration through the wood that Aurelia could feel in her own aching bones.

He didn’t touch her; he knew better than to invade her space while she was still bleeding from the inside, but his proximity was overwhelming. He leaned in close enough that his breath stirred the stray hairs damp with sweat at her temple, and his voice dropped to a murmur that required no effort to hear.
"You are exhausted," he said. His tone was devoid of pity; it was worse.

It was a simple statement of fact, delivered with the clinical precision of a surgeon. "You have spent seven days holding back a flood, managing a crisis that would have shattered a dozen lesser men before they even reached the breaking point.
’Exhaustion has a way of eroding even the most solid ground, turning certainties into shadows..."
"What you are feeling right now isn’t weakness, Aurelia... It is simply the inevitable collapse of a body that has been asked to carry more than any one person was ever designed to bear."
Aurelia stiffened, her jaw clenching so hard she feared her teeth might crack.
"Do not manage me, Rex," she spat, but the venom was gone.
The words lacked the bite of her earlier rage; they sounded hollow, the desperate protest of someone who was already drowning. "I am not one of your twelve subordinates."
"I am not some asset to be steadied or a problem to be solved... I do not need you to talk me down from a difficult morning."
"I am not managing you," Rex countered immediately, his voice cutting through her protest with terrifying calm. "I am speaking the truth."
"And the truth is that you have spent thirty years cultivating a persona of invulnerability."
"You have made it your life’s work to be the strongest person in every room, the unshakable foundation upon which this entire household rests."
He shifted slightly, his shadow engulfing her. "But this week has demanded more than even that legendary strength was built to provide."

"This week has demanded a price." His eyes locked onto hers, unblinking. "Locking Theo away in that room, striking him until your own hands bled, coming here in the dead of night to punish a training post because you have nowhere else to put the fury—none of that makes you weak."
"None of that makes you less of a leader."
He paused, letting the silence of the training hall press in around them, thick with the metallic tang of her blood and the unspoken horrors of the evening.

"It makes you human, Aurelia," he said softly, each word landing like a hammer blow. "Which is something I suspect you haven’t permitted yourself to not be in front of your staff, not in front of your son, and certainly not in front of me for a very long time."

Something in Aurelia’s composure, that ironclad fortress she had spent three decades constructing, finally shattered. The admission of her own humanity had cracked the foundation, and now the walls were crumbling.

When she looked at Rex, the expression beneath her gaze was raw, terrifyingly unguarded, and stripped of every aristocratic pretense. She didn’t look like a matriarch; she looked like a wounded animal seeking a worthy adversary.
"Spar with me," she commanded, though the words came out as something closer to a plea. "One last time..."
"Properly."

chapters.title: Chapter 984. Spar With Me, She Pleaded, Punching Where Words Failed
paragraphs: Her voice took on a desperate edge, cutting through the stale air of the hall. "I do not want to talk about Theo."
"I do not want to hear about Tremor, or conspiracies, or the lies that are rotting this house from the inside out."
"I want to hit something that will actually hit back..."

"I want to feel the impact of a blow that doesn’t break. And I want it to be you, Rex... because you are the only person left in this godforsaken household strong enough that I do not have to hold back."
Rex studied her for a long moment. He saw the tremor in her hands, the way her pupils were blown wide with adrenaline and grief.

He knew that if he refused, she would either collapse or destroy herself against the training post. He stepped back into the center of the open floor, rolling his shoulders, his stance shifting from passive observer to lethal combatant.
"Come then," he said, his voice dropping into the low, focused register of a man preparing for violence.
She exploded toward him.
There was no warm-up, no measured approach. Aurelia launched herself at him with a ferocity that made the air whistle.

Every ounce of her accumulated rage, every sleepless hour spent wondering if her son was a monster, and every drop of blood she had spilled that morning was channeled into a single, devastating opening gambit.
Her strikes were clean decades of flawless mastery holding her form together, but they were fueled by a desperation that bordered on suicidal.
Rex met her in the center of the ring. He didn’t match her recklessness; foolishness got you killed, but he matched her intensity.
When her fist connected with his forearm in a lightning-fast jab, the impact sounded like a hammer hitting stone.
When he countered with a controlled elbow to her ribs, he felt the solid, terrifying strength behind her movement.

The engagement stretched on, becoming a brutal dance of bone against bone. The training hall echoed with the wet slap of skin, the grinding of teeth, and the ragged, guttural sounds of two people pushed to their physical limits.

Aurelia was relentless. She pressed sequence after sequence, spinning back fists; delivered devastating knee strikes; and palm-heeled aimed at his solar plexus, each one delivered with the intent to maim.
She wasn’t fighting to win a point; she was fighting to exorcise a demon.
’Strike. Breathe. Strike. Breathe.’
Her inner monologue was a storm of static: ’Hit him. Break something.’
’Make the pain outside match the pain inside.’
’Don’t stop. If I stop, the truth catches up.’
’If I stop, I have to face what I did to Theo.’
She was magnificent and terrifying. But grief is a poison that clouds even the sharpest mind. As the minutes ticked by, her technique began to fray at the edges.

The fury that gave her strength was also eating her discipline. She became aggressive in ways that were surgically precise but tactically suicidal, leaving microfractures in her defense gaps that a lesser fighter would have died in.
Rex saw them. He saw the way her weight shifted too heavily on her left foot during a roundhouse kick; he saw the way she lowered her chin when she lunged for a finishing blow.
More than once, he could have shattered her ribs with a precise counter or swept her legs to end the fight instantly. But he didn’t.
He chose not to exploit the openings. He allowed her to work through the exchange on her own terms, playing the role of the immovable object so she could continue to be the unstoppable force.
He was giving her the only thing she could still understand: a struggle she could control.
Then came the breaking point.

Exhaustion finally breached her defenses. Aurelia committed to a vicious three-part combination: left hook, right cross, and spinning elbow, the same sequence that had served her so well throughout the night.
But on the final rotation, her foot slipped fractionally on a patch of sweat and blood on the mat. Her balance shifted too far forward, her center of gravity betraying her.
Rex caught the moment with predatory timing. He didn’t strike her; he simply moved.

As she came spinning into the space where he had been, he stepped inside her arc and redirected her momentum with the cold efficiency of a lever. He planted his foot and executed a controlled, devastating sweep.
The world tilted violently for Aurelia. Her legs were swept from under her, and her own momentum carried her downward like a felled oak.
She hit the reinforced wooden floor hard, a bone-jarring impact that sent a shockwave through her spine and forced every last molecule of air from her lungs in a strangled wheeze.

She lay there, sprawled on the polished boards, the silence of the hall rushing back in to fill the space where her fury had been. Her chest heaved in violent, shuddering spasms as she fought to reclaim her breath.

Her raw, split knuckles rested against the wood, stained dark with blood, while she simply stared up at the high stone ceiling, watching the moonlight dance across the rafters while the echoes of the fight died away in the hollow ache of her bones.

Rex crossed the blood-slicked distance between them, each footfall heavy against the floorboards that still hummed with the violence of their exchange. He didn’t tower over her; instead, he knelt beside her, bringing himself down to her level.
Slowly, deliberately, he extended his hand. His knuckles were scraped and his forearm bore the angry red welts where her strikes had landed, but his grip remained unshakable.
Aurelia stared at his outstretched palm. For several heartbeats, she didn’t move, her pupils dilated as she stared at the hand that had just been her adversary.
Her breathing was still a series of ragged, wet gasps. Then, with a tremor she couldn’t quite suppress, she reached up and grasped it.
When he pulled her up, the movement was deceptively gentle. He anchored her as she found her footing, steadying her against the dizziness that follows such primal exertion.
For several long moments, they simply stood there, two predators caught in the aftermath of a hunt, their bodies close enough to share heat.
The space between them wasn’t empty; it was charged, vibrating with the residual adrenaline and the raw, bleeding truths they had just hammered out of each other.
Aurelia finally turned her gaze toward him, and the look she gave him was devastating. It wasn’t anger, nor was it gratitude.

It was a weary, corrosive disgust, a self-directed contempt that seemed to seep from her bones. It was the expression of a woman who had just realized she had exposed her most vulnerable nerve to someone who might not be worthy of seeing it.
"I hate how much better I feel," she whispered, her voice cracking like dried parchment. "I hate that after all that... after all that violence... I feel lighter.
"I hate that doing this with you was more effective than any hour I spent alone."
"That is not something to hate, Aurelia," Rex said. His voice was a low rumble in the cavernous hall, steady as a heartbeat.
"Is it not?" she challenged, a bitter laugh catching in her throat. "I have spent thirty years being the pillar."

Her strikes were clean decades of flawless mastery holding her form together, but they were fueled by a desperation that bordered on suicidal.
Rex met her in the center of the ring.
He didn’t match her recklessness; foolishness got you killed, but he matched her intensity.

The fury that gave her strength was also eating her discipline.

Rex saw them.
